summary: The README of Emil Kowalski's skills repository explains why the skills exist and lists what each one does. Its core argument is that AI agents lack taste: they pick ease-in for an enter animation where ease-out is right, or a solid border where a semi-transparent shadow is right, and these small mistakes compound. The skills encode the author's experience at Vercel and Linear as lists of such mistakes and their fixes, so agents reach the right design and animation decisions faster. It frames AI as an amplifier of domain expertise, not a replacement. For a design system, it supplies two concrete defaults (ease-out for enter, shadows over solid borders), a map of which skill handles which job (build, review, audit, find opportunities, name effects, pick libraries, prototype, mobile polish), and the install command.
key_ideas: Knowing whether an animation or design choice is right is hard; these skills aim to shorten the path to the right decision.
AI agents do not have great taste and often pick the wrong ingredients for an animation.
Enter animations should use ease-out; agents often wrongly use ease-in.
A semi-transparent shadow is the better choice where agents reach for a solid border.
Small wrong choices compound until an interface is either amazing or just not that great.
The skills list the small mistakes agents make and explain how to fix them.
AI amplifies domain expertise rather than replacing it, so learning to code or design stays valuable.
Each skill covers one job: build an animation, review strictly, audit a codebase, find where motion helps, name effects, pick a library, prototype variants, or make web apps feel native on phones.
Agents should use trusted libraries instead of hand-rolling components like toasts or installing abandoned packages.

rules.rule: Use ease-out, not ease-in, for enter animations.
rules.why: The README names ease-in on an enter animation as one of the little mistakes agents make, when it is 'supposed to be ease-out'; the reason itself is in the linked 7 Practical Animation Tips article, not in the README.
rules.evidence: An `ease-in` easing for an enter animation

rules.rule: Prefer a semi-transparent shadow over a solid border in UIs (the README gives no narrower scope or values).
rules.why: Choosing a solid border instead of a semi-transparent shadow is one of the small agent mistakes that compound.
rules.evidence: solid border instead of a semi-transparent shadow

rules.rule: Pick the library for a task from libraries the author uses and trusts, instead of letting an agent hand-roll a component such as a toast or install an abandoned package.
rules.why: The pick-ui-library skill exists so the agent picks the right library instead of hand-rolling a toast component or installing an abandoned package.

rules.rule: When building an animation from scratch, explicitly choose its curve, duration and properties.
rules.why: The animate skill exists to pick the correct curve, duration and properties.

rules.rule: Add motion only where it genuinely benefits the UI, and state explicitly what should not be animated.
rules.why: find-animation-opportunities searches for places that would genuinely benefit from motion while also saying what not to animate.

rules.rule: Review animations strictly against the author's rules.
rules.why: review-animations reviews animations in a strict way based on the author's rules.

rules.rule: When auditing a codebase's animations, produce prioritized, self-contained plans that any agent can execute.
rules.why: improve-animations audits all animations and returns prioritized, self-contained plans.

rules.rule: Describe an animation to an AI with its exact term rather than a vague description.
rules.why: Using the right words gets better animations from an AI.
rules.evidence: telling it exactly what you want by using the right words

rules.rule: Build several different versions of a UI piece you describe and go through them with a switcher.
rules.why: The prototype skill builds multiple versions of a described UI piece to go through with a switcher.

rules.rule: When a web app runs on a phone, fix sticky hover states, tap highlight flashes, the 100vh bug, inputs that zoom the page, laggy taps and safe areas.
rules.why: These small fixes separate a website from an app and make it feel native on a phone.

rules.rule: In React Native and Expo, hold gestures, sheets, haptics and screen transitions to the same bar as the other animation skills, and keep motion off the JS thread.
rules.why: animate-expo is described as 'the same bar' for React Native and Expo, and names keeping motion off the JS thread.

rules.rule: Write modern Swift: value types, Swift 6 concurrency, generics, attention to performance, and Swift Testing.
rules.why: The write-swift skill defines modern Swift by these practices.

rules.rule: Keep developing real design or engineering expertise and use AI to amplify it, not to replace it.
rules.why: The skills are a side-effect of domain expertise; AI amplifies expertise and makes you better relative to others.
rules.evidence: So learn to code, design, or develop expertise

caveats: Contains self-promotion: a newsletter signup at animations.dev/skills and a header image linking to animations.dev.
The README only summarizes each skill; the detailed rules live in the individual skill files, which are separate sources.
The skill list and install command reflect commit 85e8e23 and may change.
The authority rests on the author's experience at Vercel and Linear, not on cited studies.
write-swift is a general coding skill, not a design rule; it is kept for iOS projects only.
The README states that enter animations should be ease-out but not why; the reason is in the linked 7 Practical Animation Tips article, a separate source.
The shadow-over-border example gives no scope (which elements) and no values (opacity, blur), so it is recorded as a should, not a locked must; the detailed rule should come from the skill files.

Skill descriptions are summaries of what each skill does, so the rules drawn from them (review strictly, audit into plans, name effects, prototype variants) are recorded as should or consider, not must.
